data.claim: A reviewer chunk whose first copy returns DID NOT CONVERGE (or TRUNCATED) is deterministically doomed: a hedge copy is the same chunk with the same budget and timeout, so it must fail identically. Cancelling the hedge twin and settling the chunk at once stops a lost chunk waiting hedge x timeout_s.
data.falsifier: The hedge copy succeeds where the first copy DID NOT CONVERGE (an identical request converging on retry under identical budget/timeout).
data.mechanism: In review._race, a queued hedge copy started only after the first timed out (max_concurrency=1 queues it), so a non-converging chunk burned hedge x timeout_s before reporting DID NOT CONVERGE, while the progress tick claimed each request is cut at timeout_s.
data.probe: Reviewer(kind=command, hedge=2, timeout_s=2, max_concurrency=1) over one non-splitting chunk that sleeps 20s: with the twin cancelled the review runs the command ONCE (seen.txt==1); without it, twice (seen.txt==2).

data.question: Does a hedge copy of a chunk whose first copy returned DID NOT CONVERGE ever converge, or is it a deterministic repeat of the same timeout?

evidence.note: Read standing rules from ddflow brief (r-gemini-key-load, r-bounded-everything, r-unavailable-not-pass, r-one-complexity, r-derive-dont-store). Applied: cancel a deterministically-doomed chunk hedge twin (bounded), load GEMINI_API_KEY before gemini review, record not passed for what cannot run, extract _cancel_twins to bound _race CC.

In review._race, a chunk whose first settled copy returns _retryable (TRUNCATED/DID_NOT_CONVERGE) now settles at that failure and cancels its hedge twins (via _cancel_twins) instead of letting a queued twin start after the first timeout and spend the same timeout_s again; _retry_truncated still halves it. Commit 884e15a15 + 39f27d743.

chunk_findings.detail: The fix assumes that `tokens[(i, other)].cancel()` will always stop a queued hedge copy, but `Future.cancel()` cannot stop a future that has already begun executing. With a concurrency-limited scheduler, when the first copy’s future completes (here, by timeout), the worker/scheduler can start the next queued copy before the main loop records `settled[i]` and calls `_cancel_twins`. The added test is exactly exposed to this race: `max_concurrency=1`, `timeout_s=2`, and the fake reviewer sleeps 20. If the queued twin starts before `settled` is set, it writes a second `x` and the round waits another timeout; `assert len(seen.read_text().split()) == 1` becomes nondeterministic and the claimed “cut at timeout_s” bound is not enforced.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/review/runner.py:_cancel_twins

chunk_findings.detail: The new branch makes the first retryable copy terminal even while other hedge copies are still expected (`left[i] > 0`). If one copy returns a retryable error such as a timeout and another copy would return a valid review slightly later (a flaky endpoint or non-deterministic model response), processing the failure first sets `settled[i]` to the failure and the other copy is cancelled/ignored, so `review()` can report the chunk unreviewed/`UNAVAILABLE` despite a successful hedge copy. The previous behavior waited for remaining hedge copies and could accept the success; this change removes the hedge protection for exactly the transient case hedge is meant to cover.

data.probe: CONFIRMED: the first cut (commit 884e15a15) cancelled the queued twin via _cancel_twins but attempt() only re-checked , so a queued twin could still start and re-time-out before the cancel landed (nondeterministic test). Fixed in 31f0e55d0: attempt() now re-reads tokens[(i,c)].cancelled first, so a cancelled-but-queued twin returns None. data.title: ddflow/services/review/runner.py:_cancel_twins

data.probe: REFUTED: a hedge copy races to WIN (first on-contract answer), it does not retry a timeout. A twin that runs IN PARALLEL started together with the timed-out copy, so it is bounded by the SAME timeout_s -- it either converges in time (and settles first, as success) or ties the SAME DID NOT CONVERGE; it has no later window to win. The twin that could start LATER is the QUEUED copy, which re-runs the deterministic failure, is now cancelled, and _retry_truncated halves it. So nothing a live twin could have won is lost.
data.title: ddflow/services/review/runner.py:elif _retryable(err)

chunk_findings.detail: The new `elif _retryable(err)` branch treats a timeout as a deterministic property of the chunk and immediately settles the chunk as failed, cancelling the other hedge copies. That is wrong when a timeout is transient. Given `Reviewer(hedge=2, timeout_s=2, max_concurrency=1)` and a fake reviewer command that sleeps past `timeout_s` on its first invocation but returns a valid review on its second invocation, the first copy times out, the new branch sets `settled[i]` to the timeout failure, and `_cancel_twins` prevents the queued second copy from ever running. The second copy would have succeeded, but `review` returns the chunk as unreviewed/DID NOT CONVERGE even though a hedge copy was available. The added regression test uses a command that always sleeps, so it only proves the copy is cancelled; it does not show that cancelling is safe for the transient timeouts hedge copies are meant to survive.
